rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the verse permits two grammatical parses, which he distinguishes on the following page.
rows.anchor: Grammatically this verse can be interpreted in two ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parse treats the opening clause about disbelievers as introductory and begins the actual subject with the person intending wrongdoing in the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: to be introductory and the actual inchoative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative parse supplies an omitted predicate, ‘then they committed a great injustice.’
rows.anchor: The second is to regard an enunciative to the effect

rows.speaker: Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī prefers the first grammatical interpretation.
rows.anchor: prefers the first of these

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi inclines to the second interpretation and translates in accordance with it.
rows.anchor: I am more inclined to the second, and my translation is in accordance with it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the parses differ, their implications are not substantially different.
rows.anchor: in both cases, the implication of the verse will not be much different.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh rejected the Prophet’s message, forcibly obstructed Muslims from God's religion, and barred them from visiting the House.
rows.anchor: who had rejected the message of the Prophet (sws) and were also trying to forcibly stop Muslims from the religion of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Equal access to the Sacred Mosque rebukes Quraysh and Banū Hāshim for monopolizing entry; no tribe may bar anyone who comes to worship, regardless of origin.
rows.anchor: No one has the right to restrict the entry of any person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The House’s residents should serve its visitors and make it a worship and pilgrimage centre for the world, as Ishmael did, rather than act as rulers.
rows.anchor: their status is not of its rulers and monopoly-holders; they are in the capacity of those who do i‘tikāf in it and serve all those who visit it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh inverted their custodial duty: instead of cleansing the House of idolatry, they filled it with what Abraham and Ishmael were told to remove.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh were guilty of stuffing the House of God with all the filth they had been asked to cleanse it from.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Muslim may be barred only if he uses the House against Abraham’s purpose for its construction.
rows.anchor: except if it is proven that he is using the House of God against the objectives for which it has been built by Abraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All Muslims share responsibility for protecting the House, and the world’s Muslims must restrain custodians who corrupt it with the very practices it was meant to be cleansed of.
rows.anchor: it is the responsibility of all the Muslims of the world to stop them from this excess.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every Muslim shares the duty to defend the House if an enemy attacks it.
rows.anchor: the responsibility of defending and protecting it is the right of every Muslim of the world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treaties or expediency cannot excuse abandoning this duty; believers must oppose even a nominally Muslim government that prevents people from taking part in its defence.
rows.anchor: it will be obligatory upon the believers to wage jihād against it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The House is the heart of the Muslim community, whose unity and stability depend on it.
rows.anchor: It is the heart of the Muslim ummah.

rows.speaker: Our jurists
rows.claim: Jurists infer that no one may own a house or collect rent within the Ḥaram precincts.
rows.anchor: Our jurists have also inferred from them that within the precincts of the Ḥaram none can own a house or receive rent from someone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects that inference as unfounded; the equality phrase describes the House itself, not all of Makkah or the Ḥaram.
rows.anchor: I regard this inference to be unfounded.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi sides with the Shāfiʿīs, who oppose the restriction on owning or renting property in the Ḥaram.
rows.anchor: I would give preference to view of the Shafites who are not in favour of this restriction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition before al-ilḥād makes yurīd encompass the sense of intending or resolving.
rows.anchor: shows that this verb encompasses the meaning of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ilḥād means deviation or irreligion.
rows.anchor: means deviation and being irreligious.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bi-ẓulmin is appositional to bi-al-ilḥād and is commonly used in the Qur’an for polytheism.
rows.anchor: and it is commonly used for polytheism in the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse threatens painful punishment for anyone who intends a grave irreligious act, such as polytheism, in the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: if a person intends to do something irreligious and that too as grave as polytheism in it, God will make him taste a painful torment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yurīd denotes an intention formed through thought, whereas hamm can be impulsive; the author illustrates the latter from 9:74 and 12:24.
rows.anchor: The former refers to the intention that has a whole thought process behind it while the latter to an intention that may be impulsive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sanctuary’s etiquette is so strict that even fleeting intentions are accountable.
rows.anchor: Even impulsive and transient intentions are held accountable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding bi-ẓulmin shows that even slight deviation is punished, making the Quraysh’s polytheism all the more indefensible.
rows.anchor: deviation will punished, how can polytheism which is the greatest oppression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage recounts Abraham and the House to show that Quraysh had ruined the House’s purpose and deserved to be displaced in favour of those worthy of it.
rows.anchor: they had totally ruined all the objectives for which Abraham (sws) and Ishmael (sws) had built it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabwiyah means making someone inhabit or populate a place; the lām indicates the site was for Ishmael and his descendants as well as Abraham.
rows.anchor: this place was not just reserved as an abode for Abraham (sws). It was also meant to be the place of residence of Ishmael

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Jews altered or removed Torah testimony linking Abraham to the House, hoping to deny the final Prophet’s Ishmaelite lineage; they recast Abraham’s migration and the intended sacrificial son as Isaac.
rows.anchor: the Jews had conspired to obliterate from the Torah or alter its verses which bore testimony to the relationship of Abraham (sws) with the House of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the Jews also altered accounts of Marwah, Makkah, and the House, but the history is too evident to conceal and Torah testimonies still expose the conspiracy.
rows.anchor: However, how could they succeed in hiding the actual history that was more radiant than the sun?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi cites Farāhī’s book on the son offered for sacrifice and his own discussion at relevant points, including his explanation of 2:141–142.
rows.anchor: My mentor Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī has done precisely this in his book Al-Rā’ī al-ṣaḥīḥ fī man huwa al-dhabīḥ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The House-purification directive parallels 2:125, which commands Abraham and Ishmael to purify it for worshippers.
rows.anchor: is almost the same as what is mentioned in the following verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This section explains Abraham’s purpose and the House’s directives to expose Quraysh’s tyrannical control and their resistance to those reviving its purpose.
rows.anchor: they have a tyrannical control of this House and are stopping those want to once again revive this real objective.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rijālan is the plural of rajul and means pedestrians.
rows.anchor: The word رﺟَﺎلٌ is the plural of ر ﺟﻞand refers to pedestrians.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍāmir describes a camel or horse made frail by a long journey and is used of either sex.
rows.anchor: means a camel or a horse that has become frail because of journeying for a long distance. It is used equally for both the male and the female gender.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added feminine marker emphasizes the term, as in the example ‘he is a brilliant scholar.’
rows.anchor: The word 9 is meant to emphasize it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fajj is a path between mountains, while ʿamīq qualifies it; narrow mountain passes deepen through repeated travel.
rows.anchor: refers to the path between mountains, and the attribute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the earlier directive to establish the House, Abraham is now told to proclaim pilgrimage so people come from near and far; this highlights Quraysh’s failure to invite all humanity and their monopolizing the House.
rows.anchor: this verse mentions the second directive: he should proclaim among people that they should come for the pilgrimage of this House

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The response to the command is a glad tiding for Abraham: after his proclamation pilgrims will come on foot and on camels, which will grow frail, while continual traffic deepens the routes.
rows.anchor: they form glad tidings for Abraham (sws): as soon as he will proclaim this invitation among people, they will come on foot and on the backs of camels to do the pilgrimage of the House.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: History confirms the imagery of abundant pilgrimage: over millennia the roads and pilgrimage sites have borne witness to growing numbers and zeal, with modern transport joining the journey.
rows.anchor: The abundance of pilgrims and their immense passion and zeal that is evident from these metaphors is borne out by history as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context shows God wills an ever-growing eagerness to visit the House, while Muslim governments impose visas, quotas, and balloting to earn foreign exchange.
rows.anchor: The context of these verses shows that it is the will and liking of God
